explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm opens with "O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength. How greatly he exults in Your salvation!" (Psalm 21:1). Notice who the strength belongs to. The king is cheering for what the LORD has, and he's not bragging about his own muscles. Honestly, I'd cheer too if I had that kind of backup.

I get why you'd think so, since a king has plenty to flex about. But the psalm says something different. It says, "O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength." (Psalm 21:1). His joy points at the LORD's strength, and his own arms don't get a mention.

An army sounds like a fair guess for a king. But the psalm never mentions one in this verse. It says, "O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength." (Psalm 21:1). He's exulting in the LORD's strength and in His salvation. Soldiers don't show up in the opening line at all.

Careful, friend, the psalm says the opposite. David tells the LORD, "You have granted his heart’s desire and have not withheld the request of his lips." (Psalm 21:2). The king's heart's desire was granted, and the request of his lips was not withheld. That's a whole lot of yes.

Right, it's false. The psalm says the LORD "…granted his heart’s desire…" and "…have not withheld the request of his lips." (Psalm 21:2). The heart's desire and the spoken request both got an answer. Then comes that Selah, which feels like a spot to stop and let it sink in.

That's right, baker! "You placed on his head a crown of pure gold." (Psalm 21:3). Pure gold, no mixing it with anything cheaper. Meanwhile my chef's hat is a tall piece of white cloth, and I still think I look sharp in it.

A helmet sounds sensible, I'll give you that. But it's not what the psalm says. The LORD welcomed the king with rich blessings, and "You placed on his head a crown of pure gold." (Psalm 21:3). Gold crown, not bronze helmet. This is a welcome with blessings, and nothing in the verse mentions armor.

Fine linen is a classy guess, and I'd happily wear it to a bakery opening. But the verse says, "You placed on his head a crown of pure gold." (Psalm 21:3). It comes right after the LORD welcomed the king with rich blessings. No turban in sight, just gold, and I bet it outshines my chef's hat.

explanations.answer: Length of days forever and ever
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The psalm says, "He asked You for life, and You granted it—length of days, forever and ever." (Psalm 21:4). He asked for life and got it with no end date on it. A king asks for life, and the answer is forever and ever.

Seventy years is a long stretch, but the psalm goes way past it. The verse says, "He asked You for life, and You granted it—length of days, forever and ever." (Psalm 21:4). Forever and ever doesn't fit inside seventy years. It's not even close.

That one adds a time limit, and the verse doesn't mention one. It says, "He asked You for life, and You granted it—length of days, forever and ever." (Psalm 21:4). The life granted is length of days, forever and ever. Tying it to his enemies falling is a plot twist the verse never writes.

That's it, friend. The psalm says, "For You grant him blessings forever; You cheer him with joy in Your presence." (Psalm 21:6). The blessings are forever, and the joy happens in the LORD's presence. That's the place the verse names.

The enemies come up later in the psalm, so I see where that came from. But this verse puts the joy somewhere else. "You cheer him with joy in Your presence." (Psalm 21:6). The cheering happens in the LORD's presence. A battlefield isn't named here.
Fair guess, friend, but this verse doesn't go there. It says, "You cheer him with joy in Your presence." (Psalm 21:6). The LORD's presence is the place the verse gives. No gate is mentioned.

Not quite, baker. David says the opposite: "For the king trusts in the LORD…" (Psalm 21:7). No horses and no chariots get mentioned in that verse. The king puts his trust in the LORD, and that's the whole answer.

Correct, it's false. The psalm says, "For the king trusts in the LORD; through the loving devotion of the Most High, he will not be shaken." (Psalm 21:7). The trust goes to the LORD. Horses and chariots never show up in this verse.

Yes, baker, shaken is the word. The verse says the king trusts in the LORD. Then it says, "through the loving devotion of the Most High, he will not be shaken." (Psalm 21:7). I've been shaken plenty, mostly by a drawer sliding open. But that's a different story.

Proud is a believable guess after all that gold and glory. But the verse says something else: "…he will not be shaken." (Psalm 21:7). It happens through the loving devotion of the Most High. The word is shaken, and pride isn't in the line.

Silent doesn't fit this verse, friend. The psalm says, "through the loving devotion of the Most High, he will not be shaken." (Psalm 21:7). The steadiness comes through the Most High's loving devotion. Nobody is hushing anybody here. The psalm is a song, after all.
True, baker. The psalm says, "Though they intend You harm, the schemes they devise will not prevail." (Psalm 21:11). They can plan all they want. The psalm says those schemes won't win.

Not this time, friend. The psalm says, "Though they intend You harm, the schemes they devise will not prevail." (Psalm 21:11). So the enemies do plan harm, but their schemes don't come out on top. It's true, and the plans don't prevail.
That's right, baker. "For You will put them to flight when Your bow is trained upon them." (Psalm 21:12). The bow is trained on them, and they're put to flight. The word to remember is flight.
Shame is a fair guess, but it's not the word here. The verse says, "…You will put them to flight when Your bow is trained upon them." (Psalm 21:12). The word is flight. Flight means running away.

Silence is a decent guess, but it's not the word here. The verse says, "…You will put them to flight when Your bow is trained upon them." (Psalm 21:12). Flight means running away. With a bow aimed at them, they'd be moving, and quickly.

Yes, baker! The psalm ends, "Be exalted, O LORD, in Your strength; we will sing and praise Your power." (Psalm 21:13). It started with the king rejoicing in the LORD's strength. It ends with "we" singing about that same power. Nice way to close a song.

Building sounds like a big, holy plan, but it's not in this line. The psalm ends, "we will sing and praise Your power." (Psalm 21:13). Singing and praising is the promise. No hammers are mentioned, only voices.

The verses just before talk about enemies, so I see why you went there. But the last line changes direction. It says, "we will sing and praise Your power." (Psalm 21:13). The "we" sings and praises. No marching is mentioned.
